docs.title: Wild Discovery And Loot
docs.text: seed_acquisition.json controls non-command crop discovery.

docs.title: Grass Drops
docs.text: Grass drops use a base chance plus biome modifiers. The bundled config makes lettuce and onion common in plains/meadows, tomato more common in forests, corn more common in plains/savanna, and rice more common in swamp/jungle-style areas.

docs.title: Chest Loot
docs.text: Village, farm, dungeon, mineshaft, and temple loot tables can receive Heirloom crop items or seed packets. The chance is per generated chest, not a guarantee for every structure.

docs.title: World Generation
docs.text:
Natural patches are placed in new chunks only. Ground crops are the safest candidates. Vine crops need walls, and aquatic crops need water placement, so test those carefully before enabling broad worldgen.

Warning

World generation and chest loot only affect newly generated or newly filled content. Use commands, seed packets, or custom events if you need to seed old worlds.

docs.title: First Farm
docs.text: Start with Lettuce because it uses the simplest plant type.

docs.title: Crop Examples
docs.text: Lettuce: Short ground crop. Onion: Allium-style ground crop. Corn: Tall crop with vertical room. Tomato: Wall vine crop. Rice: Aquatic crop planted in water.

docs.title: Get A Crop Item
docs.text:
Admins can test with:

/hl give LETTUCE

Players normally discover seeds through grass drops, seed packets, chest loot, or world generation, depending on server configuration.

docs.title: Plant Lettuce
docs.text:
1. Hold LETTUCE.
  2. Right-click grass, dirt, coarse dirt, podzol, or rooted dirt.
  3. Wait for the display to mature.
  4. Right-click the mature crop to harvest.

docs.title: Try The Other Core Crops
docs.text:
• Lettuce: short ground plant.
  • Onion: allium-style ground plant.
  • Corn: tall plant.
  • Tomato: wall vine.
  • Rice: aquatic crop planted in water above soil.

See Gardening for conditions, permissions, and drops.

docs.title: First Meal
docs.text: This walkthrough makes a simple cooked food and teaches the physical station flow.

docs.title: First Meal Visual Flow
docs.text: Build the Frying Pan from a furnace and heavy weighted pressure plate. Right-click with an egg to place it as a visible ingredient. Start cooking with an empty hand and watch the progress feedback. Collect the finished Fried Egg from the station.

docs.title: Common Wrong Turn
docs.text: The vanilla furnace GUI does not cook Heirloom recipes; interact with the physical station instead.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Cook Fried Egg on a Frying Pan.

docs.title: Build The Frying Pan
docs.text: Place a FURNACE, then place a HEAVY_WEIGHTED_PRESSURE_PLATE on top. The plate is the station block players interact with.

docs.title: Cook
docs.text:
1. Hold an egg.
  2. Right-click the frying pan to add it.
  3. Empty your hand.
  4. Right-click the station to begin cooking.
  5. Wait for the completion effects.
  6. Left-click to collect the result, or add more ingredients if the result is part of another recipe chain.

docs.title: What To Notice
docs.text:
• The station stores visible ingredients as display entities.
  • Some stations need tools for best results, such as chopping tools on the Cutting Board.
  • Recipe quality can improve with correct station interaction and Cooking Mastery.

Next: First Farm or Recipe Browser.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Install Heirloom Core first, then add optional gameplay addons or food packs. Cafe, Distillery, Mixology and Pasture each require Core; Cafe and Distillery are optional integrations for Mixology.

docs.title: Install Layout
docs.text: Core and addon jars beside their generated plugin folders. Generated Heirloom resource files after the first startup.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Paper server; see the compatibility table below.
  • Java version matching the server build you run.
  • Heirloom core jar.
  • Optional: HeirloomDistillery, HeirloomCafe, HeirloomOrchard (Mixology), and HeirloomPasture addon jars.
  • Optional: PacketEvents for interactive station tutorials. Cooking, crops and addons work without it.
  • Optional visual plugins: Nexo, ItemsAdder, CraftEngine, or MMOItems.
  • Optional protection plugins: WorldGuard, Towny, GriefPrevention, Lands, or similar claim plugins.

docs.title: Versions and Dependencies
docs.text:
Product Version Dependency Heirloom Core 2.11.0 Required for Heirloom gameplay Cafe 2.11.0 Use with Core 2.11.0 Distillery 2.11.0 Use with Core 2.11.0 Mixology 1.0.1 Core 2.10.1 or newer; Core 2.11.0 recommended Pasture 2.11.0 Java 21; Paper 1.21.11; Heirloom 2.10.0; matching Core candidate required Heirloom American Food Pack 1.0.1 Heirloom 2.10.1+ (shared Soda Water build) for cooking; standalone sprites need no Heirloom Heirloom Asian Food Pack 1.0.0 Heirloom 2.9+ for cooking; standalone sprites need no Heirloom

Install matching Core, Cafe and Distillery updates together. Mixology keeps the internal name HeirloomOrchard, its /hlo command and the plugins/HeirloomOrchard/ data folder. Addons do not require separate license keys when Core is active.

The current private Pasture 2.11.0 candidate requires Java 25, Paper 26.2 and its matching Core 2.11.0 candidate. Install both jars from the same candidate archive; earlier private builds can share the version label. This Pasture acceptance scope does not include Paper 1.21.11 or 26.1.2. Public Pasture publication remains gated on the candidate's release checks.

docs.title: Server Compatibility
docs.text:
Java Paper Release verification Java 21 Paper 1.21.11 Compilation and automated tests Java 25 Paper 26.2 API compilation and automated tests

Heirloom targets Java 21 bytecode. Use the Java runtime required by your Paper build. Automated checks do not establish client-side visual acceptance for optional resource packs.

docs.title: Install Core
docs.text:
1. Stop the server.
  2. Download Core from your purchasing account and put its jar in plugins/, replacing the previous Core jar.
  3. Start the server and check that Heirloom enables successfully.
  4. Confirm plugins/Heirloom/ was created.
  5. Join and run /hl help.

docs.title: Voxel Purchases
docs.text:
Voxel Core downloads activate automatically through RIC using the personalized proof included in your download. Existing buyers can re-download the current Core release from their Voxel account and replace the old jar while the server is stopped. No manual license key is needed for the normal Voxel installation.

The standard Voxel Core license is perpetual and allows three server installations. Each server creates its own installation identity. Keep that identity for updates and restarts on the same server; do not copy license-installation-id or license-lease.json into another server installation.

Core renews its signed license shortly after startup and then every two hours. Temporary connection errors allow Core to continue for the remaining validity of its current six-hour signed lease. A definitive refusal or an expired lease disables Heirloom addons and Core through their normal shutdown handlers. Restore connectivity or resolve the reported license issue, then restart the server.

If the console reports an unavailable or invalid Voxel proof, download a fresh Core jar from your Voxel account. The legacy license-key setting is not a replacement for a Voxel proof. Contact support if a fresh download still fails, including the error code and request ID from the log, without sharing license files.

docs.title: BuiltByBit and MCModels Purchases
docs.text: BuiltByBit and MCModels downloads continue to use the existing Lukittu licensing flow. Keep the license setup supplied with that marketplace download. The Voxel RIC change does not require moving those installations to a different license system.

docs.title: Install Addons
docs.text:
Stop the server, put the Cafe, Distillery, Mixology or Pasture addon jars in plugins/ beside Core, and start the server. Use the versions listed above. Mixology's downloadable jar is named HeirloomOrchard.

For the private Pasture candidate, install Heirloom-2.10.1.jar and HeirloomPasture-2.10.1.jar together on Java 25 / Paper 26.2. Pasture creates its editable config and content under plugins/HeirloomPasture/; do not copy its addon JSON into Core's folder. Check /hl → Animal Care, /hl → Pasture Cheeses, or /hlp menu. Natural animals stay wild by default; supported directly bred newborns join care. Review plugins/HeirloomPasture/config.yml and the Pasture guide. No provider package is required for its head/vanilla visuals.

Use:

/hld help
/hlc help
/hlo info

Food-pack JSON goes in plugins/Heirloom/; follow the individual pack guide for its exact files and optional provider setup. Use /hl reload for supported content edits. Restart after replacing jars or changing license credentials.

docs.title: First Files To Review
docs.text:
• plugins/Heirloom/config.yml
  • plugins/Heirloom/custom_items.json
  • plugins/Heirloom/recipes.json
  • plugins/Heirloom/crops.json
  • plugins/Heirloom/dietary_properties.json
  • plugins/Heirloom/seed_acquisition.json

docs.title: Verify The Install
docs.text:
Run /hl debug test from an admin account. It checks item registration, recipe matching, crop registration, protection hooks, EcoEnchants detection, and runtime GUI loading.

Tip

If you use a claim plugin, test planting, harvesting, and station use in both allowed and denied regions before opening the server to players.

docs.title: Recipe Browser
docs.text: The recipe browser is the main in-game guide for players.

docs.title: Open It
docs.text:
/hl
/hl recipes
/hl search pizza

/hl opens the main menu for players. /hl search <query> opens filtered results by recipe, station, addon, output, or ingredient.

docs.title: Search Examples
docs.text: Recipe search GUI filtered to useful results. Chat search output for quick recipe lookup.

docs.title: How To Read It
docs.text:
• Open Crafting for equipment, containers and supported workstation recipes. The matching runtime indexes recipes registered on your server.
  • Click a recipe to inspect inputs and output.
  • Click ingredients to follow recipe chains backward.
  • Use item-use pages to answer "what can I cook with this?"
  • Addon recipes appear only when their addon is installed and registered.

Back and Forward use left/right arrow heads to move through your browsing history. Previous Page uses an up-arrow head and Next Page uses a down-arrow head in the rightmost two slots of the bottom row: zero-based slots 43 and 44 in a 45-slot browser, or the corresponding final two slots in other inventory sizes. Ingredient Bank keeps its existing top-row controls and uses the same directional heads.

docs.title: If Something Is Missing
docs.text:
• Make sure the addon is installed.
  • Run /hl reload after JSON changes.
  • Check startup logs for recipe validation warnings.
  • Use /hl debug test for registration diagnostics.

docs.title: Player Guide
docs.text:
This section explains Heirloom as a game system rather than a config file. Read it when you want to know what a player is expected to do, what the item lore means, and why a recipe result changed.

Start with Cooking Basics, then use Recipe Search, Favourite Food, Food Quality, and Farming And Seed Discovery.

docs.title: Advancements
docs.text:
Heirloom has native advancement progress.

Heirloom tracks food discovery, crop harvesting, recipe progress, collection goals, and quality milestones.

Commands:

/hl advancements
/hl adv
/hl progress

docs.title: How Progress Is Counted
docs.text:
Eating custom foods records the food ID and quality. Harvesting crops records crop progress. Collection advancements check whether you have eaten or harvested every item in a list, while counter advancements check totals.

Admins can customize bundled advancement data in advancements.json.

docs.title: Cooking Basics
docs.text: Heirloom cooking is physical. You build a station in the world, add visible ingredients, process the station, then either collect the result or keep using that result as part of a recipe chain.

docs.title: Station Loop Example
docs.text: Ingredients are placed into the world as visible station contents. Cooking starts from the station interaction, with progress shown in game. Opening the vanilla furnace GUI is a sign you are using the wrong interaction path.

docs.title: The Station Loop
docs.text:
1. Build the correct station shape.
  2. Right-click with ingredients to place them on the station.
  3. Empty your hand and right-click to begin processing.
  4. Wait for the station effects and progress to finish.
  5. Left-click to collect the output, or keep the output in the station flow if the next recipe uses it.

docs.title: Chains Are The Point
docs.text: Many foods are not one-step crafts. Flour can become dough, dough can become bread or pancakes, rice can become cooked rice and then a meal, and jam can become a topping that carries properties into another food. When a recipe says it wants JAM, it means the actual item you made, including quality, creator data, consume returns, and food properties.

docs.title: What Changes A Result
docs.text: A finished food can be changed by recipe rules, optional ingredients, inherited properties, quality, and visual actions. That is why two foods with the same output ID can have different names, lore, textures, or effects.

docs.title: Container Returns
docs.text:
Some recipes and foods return buckets or bottles. There are two common cases:

  • Craft return: the station gives something back when the recipe completes.
  • Consume return: eating the food gives something back afterward, such as a bottle from jam.

docs.title: Common Failure Cases
docs.text:
• The station shape is wrong, so Heirloom never treats the block as a station.
  • The ingredient is the wrong form, such as WHEAT instead of BAG_OF_FLOUR.
  • The recipe belongs to another station or addon.
  • An optional ingredient matched the base recipe but not the rule you expected.
  • A protection plugin cancelled interaction in the region.

Use /hl search <ingredient> when stuck. It is usually faster than guessing the next station.

docs.title: Favourite Food
docs.text: Favourite food is a personal RPG feature. You choose one custom food, then get extra effects whenever you eat that food ID.

docs.title: Command
docs.text:
/hl favourite

Aliases:

/hl favorite
/hl fav

docs.title: What You Get
docs.text:
Eating your favourite food applies:

Effect Duration Strength Regeneration 30 seconds I Saturation 15 seconds II Luck 60 seconds I

These effects are added after normal food-property effects. If your favourite food is also a property-stacked food, both systems apply.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A plain favourite is useful. A favourite with inherited properties is stronger. For example, pancakes made with GOLDEN and CHORUS jam can apply those property effects, then the favourite-food package if pancakes are your selected favourite.

docs.title: Social Cooking
docs.text: Heirloom stores cooked-by data on edible outputs. If somebody else cooked your favourite food, the favourite check can reward the cook with a short regeneration effect. The AFFINITY food property also reads cooked-by data and becomes stronger when the food is also your favourite.

docs.title: Server Notes For Players
docs.text: If /hl favourite is unavailable, ask staff whether heirloom.favourite is granted. The feature is permission-gated so servers can decide whether it is part of default progression.

docs.title: Cooking Mastery
docs.text:
Cooking Mastery rewards repeated practice with a recipe.

Cooking Mastery tracks how often you cook each recipe. Mastery is recipe-specific: being excellent at pancakes does not automatically make you excellent at sushi.

Command:

/hl mastery

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
Level Crafts Quality bonus Novice 0 0% Apprentice 5 +5% Competent 15 +10% Skilled 30 +15% Expert 50 +20% Master 80 +30%

The bonus is added to the recipe quality roll. This makes frequently cooked foods more reliable without making every recipe globally easier.

docs.title: Placeable Foods And Feasts
docs.text:
Some foods can be placed and eaten in servings.

Some Heirloom foods can be placed and eaten in servings. The placed block stores remaining servings, remaining nutrition, remaining saturation, and food properties in block data so state survives restarts.

docs.title: How To Eat
docs.text: Right-click the placed food with an empty hand. Each bite consumes one serving and applies that serving's share of nutrition, saturation, and any stored food-property effects.

docs.title: Feasts
docs.text: Feast foods track unique participants. When a new guest joins a feast, previous participants receive a small regeneration bonus. This rewards shared meals without giving the same player repeated guest credit.

docs.title: Breaking Placed Food
docs.text: Breaking a placed food removes it and plays food-colored break particles. It does not return the whole food item.

docs.title: Food Quality
docs.text: Food quality is stored on custom foods and ingredients. It is not just flavor text: quality is part of progression, advancement tracking, and recipe identity.

docs.title: What Changes Quality
docs.text:
• Recipe actions can set a base quality or add to it.
  • Ingredient quality can carry into later foods; the crafting code keeps the best input quality when no explicit quality is supplied.
  • Crops can store quality and keep it when replanted after harvest.
  • Cooking Mastery adds a recipe-specific quality bonus as you repeat the same recipe.

docs.title: Reading Quality In Play
docs.text: Quality appears in item names and lore. If two players make the same recipe but one uses better ingredients or has more mastery, their outputs can differ.

docs.title: Quality Tooltip Example
docs.text: Quality and dietary data are visible directly in item lore.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Quality supports long-term goals: better crops, better repeated cooking, and quality-based advancements. If a recipe feels unrewarding, check whether it is setting quality too low or never inheriting quality from its ingredients.

Server owners can inspect the data side in Custom Recipes.

docs.title: Recipe Search
docs.text: /hl search <query> searches recipes by name, station, addon, ingredient, or output. It is the fastest way to follow a chain backward.

docs.title: Search Examples
docs.text:
Recipe search GUI filtered to useful results. Chat search output for quick recipe lookup.

Examples:

/hl search pizza
/hl search rice
/hl search oven
/hl search cafe
/hl search jam

docs.title: How To Use Search Well
docs.text: Search the ingredient you are holding, not only the food you want. If you have RICE, search rice to find cooked rice and later meal paths. If you have JAM, search jam to find pancakes, doughnuts, or any server-added recipes that use it.

docs.title: Recipe Detail Preview
docs.text: The in-game recipe detail view simulates the selected inputs. When a selected ingredient has food properties or dietary data, the preview can show the resulting lore before you cook it.

docs.title: Farming And Seed Discovery
docs.text: Players can obtain crop starts in several ways, depending on server settings.

docs.title: Discovery Methods
docs.text:
• Grass drops from valid grass or fern blocks.
  • Seed packets that open into weighted seed drops.
  • Chest loot in villages, dungeons, mineshafts, and temples.
  • Natural crop patches in new chunks.
  • Admin commands during testing.

docs.title: What To Try First
docs.text: Break grass in a biome that matches the crop you want, explore village/farm-style loot, then use seed packets when you find them. Rice and other special crops may be weighted toward specific biome groups rather than appearing everywhere.

docs.title: Seed Packets
docs.text:
Temperate packets focus on lettuce, corn, tomato, onion, and some vanilla crops. Tropical packets focus on rice and warm-climate vanilla seeds.

See Seed Packets for exact data.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Recipes are loaded from JSON and indexed into the in-game browser. Players usually use /hl recipes or /hl search, while server owners edit JSON files.

docs.title: How To Read Recipe Docs
docs.text:
• Station pages explain workflow and list recipes by station.
  • Default Recipe Index is the full linked lookup.
  • Recipe Chains explains common progression paths.

docs.title: Important Concepts
docs.text:
• Required and optional ingredient slots.
  • Recipe rules that change names, quality, properties, visuals, or return items.
  • Weighted outputs for recipes with chance-based results.
  • Addon recipes that appear only when their addon registers.

docs.title: Default Recipe Index
docs.text: This page is generated from the bundled recipe JSON files and addon catalogs. It is meant for lookup; the station pages explain how the systems feel in play. Optional Mixology ingredient choices are declared in the original Core recipes, which remain Core-owned.

docs.title: Recipe Chains
docs.text: Some Heirloom recipes are deliberately chained. A station result can stay on the station and become an ingredient in the next step.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text:
• Flour -> dough -> bread, pizza, pasta, pancakes, doughnuts.
  • Rice -> cooked rice -> sushi-style recipes.
  • Corn -> cornmeal -> taco shell and related recipes.
  • Coffee cherry -> light beans -> medium beans -> dark beans -> espresso drinks.
  • Green tea leaves -> dried green tea -> chance for matcha powder -> matcha latte.
  • Mixology spirits -> liqueurs, Gin, Sweet Vermouth, Red Bitter Aperitif or Aromatic Bitters -> shaken cocktails at the Mixology Table. Coffee Liqueur requires Cafe; Rum does not.

docs.title: How To Explore Chains In Game
docs.text: Use /hl search <ingredient> or click ingredients in the recipe browser. The wiki index links recipe outputs back to the recipe that creates them where possible.

docs.title: Station crafting recipes
docs.text: Use a crafting table. Each recipe makes one placeable station. Spaces in the patterns are empty slots. Ingredients are ordinary Minecraft items. Keep every empty cell clear; horizontal mirrors are accepted. The two-row boiling pot pattern can occupy either pair of rows. Planks and wooden slabs use their Minecraft tags: any member works in each marked cell, including mixed woods. Stone slabs do not qualify. The default install supplies five Core recipes. The optional addon-workstations overlay adds the other eight.

docs.title: Recipe Actions And Rules
docs.text:
Recipe actions modify output after a recipe matches.

Action Purpose SET_PROPERTY Set metadata such as display name or food_property ADD_QUALITY Add quality to output SET_QUALITY Set output quality SET_TEXTURE Change player-head texture; source-derived wiki recipe tables show distinct output variants when rules set different textures SET_VISUAL_ITEM Swap output to a provider-neutral visual item SET_RETURN_ITEM Emit a craft return; accepts a universal item reference and does not mutate the primary result SET_CONSUME_RETURN Store a consume return reference for an ordinary Heirloom primary result; invalid for provider-owned primary results

Common triggers include HAS_INPUT, HAS_ANY_INGREDIENT, HAS_ALL_INGREDIENTS, HAS_INGREDIENT_PROPERTY, HAS_ALL_INGREDIENT_PROPERTIES, and INPUT_COUNT_GTE.

docs.title: Server Owner Guide
docs.text: This section is for setup, permissions, diagnostics, claim protection, localization, updates, and operational safety.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Core uses /hl or /heirloom. Distillery uses /hld. Cafe uses /hlc.

The full command list is in Command Reference.

docs.title: Admin Commands To Know
docs.text:
/hl reload
/hl cheat
/hl give <item> [amount]
/hl debug test
/hld devmode status
/hlc list

/hl give Orange_Liqueur accepts a unique friendly alias, and tab completion includes these names. Full item IDs still work; use ORCHARD_ORANGE_LIQUEUR if an alias matches several items. Administrator drink grants receive the normal playable sample metadata.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Core files live in plugins/Heirloom/ after first startup.

File Purpose config.yml License key and locale custom_items.json Core item definitions recipes.json Core recipes crops.json Core crops dietary_properties.json Diet labels and hierarchy seed_acquisition.json Seed packets, grass drops, loot, world patches advancements.json Advancement definitions enchantment_integrations.json EcoEnchants and compatible enchantment keys lang/<locale>.yml Locale files

Run /hl reload after supported JSON and language changes. Restart after jar, dependency, or large visual-pack changes.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Use diagnostics after install, after updates, and after large config edits.

/hl debug test
/hl debug runtests
/hl debug testall

The diagnostic suite checks item registry counts, cooked-rice recipe matching, crop registration, WorldGuard hook state, EcoEnchants detection, event bypass safety, and runtime GUI loading.

Other debug tools:

/hl debug hunger
/hl debug actionbar <style>

docs.title: Language Files
docs.text:
Heirloom bundles many locale files. Set the active locale in config.yml.

locale: en

Useful commands:

/hl lang list
/hl lang missing <locale>

When making a custom translation, copy lang/en.yml, keep keys unchanged, translate only values, then run /hl reload.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Use a permission plugin such as LuckPerms on production servers.

See Permission Reference for the full list.

Recommended default grants:

/lp group default permission set heirloom.use true
/lp group default permission set heirloom.recipes true
/lp group default permission set heirloom.cookbook true
/lp group default permission set heirloom.advancements true
/lp group default permission set heirloom.favourite true
/lp group default permission set heirloom.mastery true
/lp group default permission set heirloom.tutorial true

Grant crop permissions if you keep the bundled crop permission nodes enabled.

docs.title: Region Protection
docs.text: Heirloom uses two layers for protection compatibility.

docs.title: WorldGuard
docs.text:
• Cooking station interaction checks WorldGuard INTERACT.
  • Planting and harvesting checks WorldGuard BUILD.

docs.title: Generic Claim Plugins
docs.text: Planting fires a programmatic BlockPlaceEvent; harvesting fires a programmatic BlockBreakEvent. This gives plugins such as Towny, GriefPrevention, Lands, and similar systems a normal event to cancel.

docs.title: Test Before Launch
docs.text:
In a protected region, test:

  • Planting a crop.
  • Harvesting a crop.
  • Using a cooking station.
  • Breaking a station with ingredients.

docs.title: 2.5 Notes
docs.text:
• Startup banners are standardized and quieter.
  • Recipe search is available through /hl search.
  • Nexo and ItemsAdder visual resolution now share provider-neutral visual IDs.
  • Prepared foods should no longer receive hidden hardcoded regeneration or bonus saturation.
  • Onion and Allium crop content are bundled.
  • Distillery grape crop definitions are restored.

docs.title: 2.0 Notes
docs.text:
• Region protection was rewritten around WorldGuard and standard Bukkit events.
  • Generic consume_return was added.
  • EcoEnchants replant and prospector hooks were added.
  • Seed packets and world discovery were added.
  • Native advancements, mastery, and favourite food systems were expanded.

docs.title: Update Checklist
docs.text:
1. Back up plugins/Heirloom/.
  2. Stop the server.
  3. Replace jars.
  4. Start and read startup warnings.
  5. Run /hl debug test.
  6. Review custom food balance if you previously worked around hidden effects.

docs.title: Cooking Stations
docs.text:
Stations are built from normal blocks. Players interact with the station block, while Heirloom validates the supporting structure below or nearby.

Animated Kitchen adds craftable furniture with moving parts for these stations. It is an optional installation; block-built stations continue to work.

Use /hl tutorial for private, clickable building and cooking lessons when PacketEvents is installed. See In-game Station Tutorials.

Station Build Main Role Oven Stone pressure plate on a smoker Baking, roasting, drying, long heat chains Boiling Pot Cauldron or water cauldron over a campfire or soul campfire Soups, rice, pasta, cheese, jam, wet recipes Mixing Bowl Flower pot on any stripped block Dough, creams, mixed prep, grinding-style steps Cutting Board Wooden pressure plate on any stripped block Chopping, slicing, mincing, flour and prep items Frying Pan Heavy weighted pressure plate on a furnace Eggs, pancakes, fried meals, fast heat Barista Machine Iron trapdoor above quartz stairs, with Cafe installed Cafe drink assembly Mixology Table Any wooden pressure plate on an iron block, with Heirloom Mixology installed Liqueurs and shaken drinks Juicer Upward-facing Dropper, clear Glass, any carpet; Heirloom Mixology enabled Three produce items into two bottles

docs.title: How To Think About Stations
docs.text:
Stations are not skins for one crafting menu. Each station teaches a different kind of recipe: prep stations make intermediate ingredients, heat stations transform them, and addon stations finish specialized chains. If a recipe does not match, search the ingredient and check the station before assuming the item is broken.

Each station page lists practical first recipes, common chains, and its generated recipe table.

docs.title: Animated Kitchen
docs.text:
Heirloom Animated Kitchen adds animated furniture for cooking on your server. Bake on a sliding oven tray, toss food in a skillet, stir a bowl and chop on a board. The stations use Heirloom's recipes, ingredients and quality rules.

Release candidate

This page describes the upcoming Animated Kitchen 1.0.0 candidate. Use its matching runtime and resource files together. Final download details and client acceptance will accompany the public release.

docs.title: What is included
docs.text:
The default installation contains the oven, boiling pot, frying stove, mixing bowl and cutting board. The pot and heated stations include their bases. Place the bowl and board on a counter built from ordinary blocks.

An optional overlay adds the barista machine, mixology table, juicer, farmhouse press, stomping tub, fermentation vat, distillation still and aging rack. Their cooking behavior requires the gameplay addons listed below. The aging rack belongs to Core; Distillery and Pasture supply aging recipes.

The optional menu theme covers the recipe browser's upper panel and leaves the player inventory unchanged. Players without a loaded resource pack keep ordinary menus. Core 3D Food is a separate optional pack and is not included.

docs.title: Craft and use a station
docs.text:
Open /hl and select Crafting. Choose a station to see its shaped recipe, ingredients and output. Tin Cans, Farmer's Hoes and supported crafting recipes from installed addons appear here too. Follow ingredient links to trace recipes, then use a normal crafting table to make the item. New Crafting labels fall back to English until your server supplies translations.

The menu shows recipes available on your server. Administrators can change recipes or omit optional content. The default crafting reference is generated from the installation package and lists all thirteen station recipes.

Place the station item as furniture. Leave room for moving parts; the oven needs a clear 2×2 footprint and two blocks of height. Place countertop pieces on a solid counter. Existing block-built Heirloom stations continue to work.

  • Insert ingredients with the normal Heirloom controls.
  • Empty-hand right-click works the bowl's spoon or board's cleaver. Normal shovel mixing and tool chopping remain available.
  • Empty-hand left-click collects contents.
  • Heated stations use actual recipe durations. Fire and light effects do not replace the floor or counter.
  • Jump inside the stomping tub to mash. Follow the owning addon's bottle and serving controls for fermentation and distillation.

Normal removal returns the station and its recoverable contents once. Denied removal should leave both in place. An interrupted, unfinished batch retains its inputs but restarts processing progress when loaded again. Completed outputs persist.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The target is Minecraft Java/Paper 26.2, Java 25, CraftEngine 26.9.1 and the matching Heirloom Core runtime. Different private builds can share 2.11.0, so use the release manifest and checksums to identify the matching JARs. Obtain Heirloom and CraftEngine separately; the artwork ZIP contains no plugin JARs.

Optional workstation Gameplay requirement Barista machine Heirloom Café 2.11.0 Mixology table and juicer Heirloom Mixology / HeirloomOrchard 1.0.1 Farmhouse press Heirloom Pasture 2.11.0 Stomping tub, fermentation vat, distillation still Heirloom Distillery 2.11.0 Aging rack Core 2.11.0; Distillery or Pasture for their aging recipes

Use the companion builds identified in the release manifest. Visual definitions alone do not install their gameplay addon. This package does not claim Nexo, ItemsAdder, MMOItems or Bedrock support.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Stop the server and back up worlds, plugin data and the resource pack.
  2. Install the matching runtime, retaining existing configuration and license files. Keep one JAR per plugin.
  3. Copy the ZIP's install/plugins/ contents into plugins/. This includes the CraftEngine resource folder and required Heirloom station-visuals/rustic-kitchen.json manifest.
  4. Copy optional/addon-workstations/install/plugins/ for the optional stations and install their gameplay addons.
  5. Enable CraftEngine's furniture.light-system.enable for cooking light. Set up automatic pack hosting at an address your players can reach.
  6. Start the server. Run ce reload all, then ce reload pack. Reconnect, accept the pack, and open /hl → Crafting.

docs.title: Update or remove
docs.text:
Collect batches and stored items before updating. Remove old ovens without room for the current model, then stop and back up the server. Follow the ZIP's guide to replace the dedicated workstation resource folder and external manifests together. Do not leave an old monolithic rustic_workstations.yml alongside the new Core/addon configuration files.

Restart after changing JARs or station manifests. Rebuild the pack and reconnect; avoid generic plugin hot-reloaders.

Before uninstalling, collect contents and remove furniture while both plugins are active. Stop the server, remove only Animated Kitchen resources, manifests and theme, then restart and rebuild the pack. To disable only the menu theme, remove plugins/Heirloom/gui-themes/animated-kitchen.json and restart.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Missing from Crafting: check that the provider definition, recipe and gameplay owner are installed. Missing content does not receive invented recipes.
  • Static furniture or mismatched parts: check matching JARs and external station manifests, then restart.
  • Old or missing textures: rebuild the pack, check its hosting address, reconnect and accept the update.
  • No cooking light: enable CraftEngine's furniture light system.
  • Cannot place or use: check space, permissions and claim restrictions. Test both an allowed area and a denied area before opening to players.

The download includes RECIPES.md, catalog.json, checksums, audio credits and the full installation guide. Keep its release manifest with your backup.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build a Barista Machine with an IRON_TRAPDOOR above QUARTZ_STAIRS. The Cafe addon must be installed and registered.

Cafe Barista Machine built from an iron trapdoor over quartz stairs.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: The Barista Machine pulls espresso, tea, cocoa, boba, iced drinks, and milk-based drinks from Cafe ingredients.

docs.title: How Recipes Behave Here
docs.text: The Barista Machine is Cafe's drink assembly station. Earlier Cafe steps happen on core stations: cherries roast in the Oven, leaves and powders use prep stations, and the Barista Machine turns those prepared ingredients into drinks.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text:
• Coffee cherry -> light beans -> medium beans -> dark beans -> espresso -> americano, latte, cappuccino, flat white, mocha, or iced coffee.
  • Leaves -> dried or ground tea ingredients -> green tea, black tea, sweet tea, matcha latte, or boba tea.
  • Milk bucket and oat milk variants often change names, returns, and dietary behavior.

docs.title: Good First Recipes
docs.text: Pull ESPRESSO, then make AMERICANO, then a milk drink. That proves the chain, the station, and container returns.

docs.title: What Can Go Wrong
docs.text: The station only registers when Cafe is installed. If the trapdoor and quartz stairs act like normal blocks, confirm the Cafe jar loaded, /hlc help works, and Cafe recipes appear in /hl search cafe.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build a Boiling Pot with a CAULDRON or WATER_CAULDRON over a CAMPFIRE or SOUL_CAMPFIRE.

Boiling Pot station built over a campfire. Boiling Pot cooking flow with visible station effects.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: The Boiling Pot handles wet recipes, soups, cheese, rice, pasta, and recipes that return buckets or bottles.

docs.title: How Recipes Behave Here
docs.text: The Boiling Pot is the liquid and simmering station. It handles soups, rice, pasta, cheese, jam, wet ingredient conversions, and recipes that care about buckets or bottles. It is also where property stacking becomes easy to understand: jam can become an ingredient in later foods while keeping the food properties created from its fruit.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text:
• Fruit + sugar + bottle -> JAM; glow berries, golden apples, and chorus fruit can add food properties to the jam.
  • RICE + water -> COOKED_RICE, which then feeds sushi and fried rice chains.
  • Milk bucket -> CHEESE, and milk plus vinegar can produce the alternate cheese path.
  • Distillery grain and rice wort can ferment raw; use the Boiling Pot first for full process-quality credit. Boiling does not change ABV.

docs.title: Good First Recipes
docs.text: Try COOKED_RICE, CHEESE, then JAM. Those three cover water inputs, bucket returns, bottle returns, and property-carrying ingredients.

docs.title: What Can Go Wrong
docs.text: A bucket can be either a normal Minecraft interaction or a recipe ingredient. If you are testing a recipe, interact normally with the station and avoid vanilla cauldron habits. If the output keeps the wrong flavor or property, inspect the recipe rules: properties come from matching ingredient rules and from inherited input data.

docs.text:

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build a Cutting Board with any wooden pressure plate on any STRIPPED_ block.

Cutting Board station built with a wooden pressure plate on stripped wood. Cutting Board chopping flow with visible prep interaction.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: The Cutting Board handles prep work such as flour, pasta, minced ingredients, and sliced recipe steps.

docs.title: How Recipes Behave Here
docs.text: The Cutting Board is prep work: chopping, slicing, mincing, and turning raw ingredients into precise recipe components. It is intentionally not a generic table; many recipes need the prepared form before another station accepts them.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text:
• WHEAT can become flour-style ingredients used by dough and batter chains.
  • Meat and plant alternatives can become minced or sliced components for later meals.
  • Pasta and similar prep items are made here before being boiled or cooked.

docs.title: Good First Recipes
docs.text: Start with flour or pasta prep. Those recipes teach the difference between vanilla ingredients and Heirloom intermediate items.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build a Frying Pan with a HEAVY_WEIGHTED_PRESSURE_PLATE on top of a FURNACE.

Frying Pan station built from a heavy weighted pressure plate on a furnace.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: The Frying Pan handles eggs, bacon, pancakes, fried rice, and other fast heated foods.

docs.title: How Recipes Behave Here
docs.text: The Frying Pan is fast heat. It handles eggs, bacon, pancakes, fried rice, and other foods where toppings and optional ingredients change the final item. This station is one of the clearest places to see inherited properties: a special jam used as a pancake topping can carry CHORUS, GOLDEN, or other properties into the finished pancakes.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text:
• Eggs and bacon prove the station works with simple vanilla inputs.
  • PANCAKES accept flour/cornmeal, eggs, milk, and optional toppings such as JAM, honey, or chocolate.
  • FRIED_RICE and similar recipes usually depend on rice being cooked first at the Boiling Pot.

docs.title: Good First Recipes
docs.text: Cook a plain egg, then pancakes, then pancakes with a custom jam. Compare the lore: the topping can change name, quality, return behavior, and inherited food properties.

docs.title: What Can Go Wrong
docs.text: The recipe can be valid but still produce a plain-looking result if the optional ingredient did not match the rule you expected. For example, bundled honey pancakes add honey naming, quality, and bottle return behavior; they do not add SWEET unless a recipe or custom ingredient explicitly stores that food property.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build an upward-facing DROPPER with GLASS above it and any carpet on top.

Insert three produce items, blend, then bottle the juice in two pours.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: Blend three fruit or vegetable items for ten seconds, then bottle the juice. Heirloom Mixology must be active.

docs.title: Blend And Bottle
docs.text:
Build an upward-facing DROPPER, place clear GLASS above it, and finish with any carpet. Heirloom Mixology's juice recipe enables the station. Click the glass with fruit or vegetables to insert exactly three items; repetitions and mixed produce are allowed. Empty-hand right-click starts a 200-tick blend (ten seconds). Ingredients keep the same size while resting and tumbling inside shaking glass. The completed batch appears as a low, flat liquid level until bottled. The recipe GUI has three independent ingredient selectors; its live preview reflects the selected mixture. Compare five private sound previews with /hl debug juicer 1 through 5, all, or stop; each lasts ten seconds. Pulsing Motor (5) is the default blending sound. Right-click the finished batch twice with Glass Bottles to collect two juices, one per click. The juice level halves after the first pour. No Water Bottle or earlier bottle insertion is required.

Before the first pour, left-click refunds original ingredients with their quality and provider data. After a pour, left-click discards the remainder and never returns consumed ingredients. Finished juice waits to be bottled. On interruption, unfinished blending resets; ingredients remain recoverable. The real glass stays in place for collision and protection while nearby players see its moving display.

Juice is drinkable and uses the vanilla lingering-potion appearance without a resource pack. It cannot be thrown and has no alcohol or Distillery brewing profile. Drinking returns one Glass Bottle. Food and saturation are half the combined input nutrition: round food down after summing, retain fractional saturation, and do not apply a second quality multiplier.

Juice inherits food properties and edible effects, including enchanted-apple benefits, Chorus teleport and poisonous-potato poison chance. Repeated ingredients do not multiply the same effect. Pure batches receive the fruit or vegetable name; mixed batches list their contents and blend their colors. Pure recipe ingredients require three matching produce items: adding one tomato to mixed juice does not make Tomato Juice.

Twenty-three base produce choices are available without Distillery. Registered Distillery grapes add up to five more. Existing owner-gated fruit remains gated.

docs.title: Suggested Blends
docs.text: Try apple + beetroot + carrot (ABC), apple + carrot + orange, or pineapple + orange + mango. These use the same dynamic recipe and remain Mixed Juice. Each batch yields two bottles with the current per-bottle nutrition and effects. Original ingredients are refundable only before the first pour; saved half-full batches retain one serving after restart. Older saved single-serving batches stay single-serving. Both new stations play the shared completion bell.

docs.title: Cook With Juice
docs.text:
Drink Exact shaker ingredients Bloody Mary Vodka, pure Tomato Juice, Lemon, Salt Garibaldi Red Bitter Aperitif, pure Orange Juice Virgin Mango Daiquiri Pure Mango Juice, Lemon, Sugar Virgin Banana Daiquiri Pure Banana Juice, Lemon, Sugar Shaken Piña Colada Pure Pineapple Juice, Canned Coconut Milk, Sugar

Every listed quantity is one. Juice supplies the bottle, so no extra empty bottle or Water Bottle is needed. Other input containers return once. The original Mixing Bowl Piña Colada recipe remains unchanged.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build a Mixing Bowl with a FLOWER_POT on any STRIPPED_ log, wood, stem, hyphae, or bamboo block.

Mixing Bowl station built with a flower pot on stripped wood.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: The Mixing Bowl handles dough, mixing, cold preparation, and Cafe grinding steps.

docs.title: How Recipes Behave Here
docs.text: The Mixing Bowl is for combining, folding, grinding, and cold prep. It often creates neutral intermediates that later become powerful when cooked elsewhere: dough, batter, cream, plant protein, and Cafe grinding steps all live here.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text:
• Flour and liquids become DOUGH, then the Oven or Frying Pan finishes the dish.
  • Cafe uses grinding-style recipes for tea leaves, matcha chances, and other drink prep.
  • Mixed ingredients can inherit dietary and food-property data from custom inputs, so the bowl is often where a server-owner recipe starts carrying metadata forward.

docs.title: Good First Recipes
docs.text: Use the bowl for dough and cream before testing more advanced recipe chains. These are easier to debug because their ingredients are obvious.

docs.title: What Can Go Wrong
docs.text: If a recipe looks right but does not match, check whether the input wants a custom item such as BAG_OF_FLOUR rather than vanilla WHEAT. For server owners, this station is a good place to test optional slots because it makes failures easy to see before cooking time is involved.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Place any wooden pressure plate directly on an IRON_BLOCK. Interact with the plate. Heirloom Mixology must be installed and registered.

Watch ingredients become a round of cocktails at the Mixology Table.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: Add the exact ingredients; an existing bottled ingredient supplies the drink's container. Juice supplies the bottle for the shaken Piña Colada and Virgin Daiquiris. Start shaking, wait for the eight-second cycle, then collect three drinks from the centered row. Reusable infusions and liqueurs produce one bottle.

docs.title: Shake A Drink
docs.text:
Add the exact ingredients, then start the station. Mixology reuses up to three bottles from bottled inputs for finished drinks, or one for reusable precursors. No extra Glass Bottle is required when a bottled ingredient is listed. Other emptied bottles, cans, and cream buckets are returned once. The shaken Piña Colada reuses its Pineapple Juice bottle; the coconut milk can is returned. Drinking returns one Glass Bottle. Chilled cocktails optionally accept one Ice (no quality bonus), Packed Ice (+0.10) or Blue Ice (+0.20); Core quality is capped at Perfect; ice improves the drink's single quality without changing ABV or serving volume. Spirits, liqueur production and B-52 do not accept ice. Each bundled liqueur or cocktail takes eight seconds: the metal shaker closes, shakes with the station sounds, and settles before the drink is ready to collect. The progress highlight travels through the filled part of the bar on a 16-tick cycle.

Begin with a Virgin Mango or Banana Daiquiri, selected by the pure juice in one shared recipe, or the shaken Piña Colada. These are always available. Gin, Sweet Vermouth, Red Bitter Aperitif and Aromatic Bitters join the three liqueurs as reusable ingredients. The authored Mixology catalog includes Negroni/Boulevardier, Old Fashioned/Rum Old Fashioned, Manhattan, White Lady, Bee’s Knees and Garibaldi. Cafe adds Coffee Liqueur and the Espresso Martini, Russian and B52 recipe families.

docs.title: Optional Addons
docs.text:
With no Distillery, Mixology provides all four Boiling Pot spirit recipes, including Rum without Cafe. Compatible Distillery replaces those spirits with genuine distilled bottles. Wine capability 2 additionally enables Sweet Vermouth from genuine Wine or Champagne plus Vodka, and its Negroni/Boulevardier and Manhattan recipes. Capability 1 retains the other alcoholic recipes. An enabled Distillery without even the spirit integration hides the alcoholic menu; the four non-alcoholic recipe families still produce five named drinks. Cafe controls the coffee branch independently.

See Heirloom Mixology for the complete mode table and source requirements. The existing Mixing Bowl Piña Colada recipe remains available.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build an Oven with a STONE_PRESSURE_PLATE on top of a SMOKER.

Oven station built from a stone pressure plate on a smoker.

docs.title: Core Loop
docs.text: The Oven handles baking, roasting, drying, and some chain steps such as bread, pizza, and coffee roasting.

docs.title: How Recipes Behave Here
docs.text: The Oven is the long-form heat station. It is where raw prep becomes shelf-stable or baked food: dough becomes bread, flat dough becomes pizza, wet coffee cherries become roast beans, and some addon chains use it as the first serious processing step.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text:
• BAG_OF_FLOUR -> DOUGH -> bread, pizza, pancakes, waffles, doughnuts, and pastry-style recipes.
  • Cafe coffee cherries roast through light, medium, and dark beans before they become espresso drinks.
  • Recipes with SET_RETURN_ITEM can give containers back after the craft, so check the output and your inventory before assuming a bucket or bottle vanished.

docs.title: Good First Recipes
docs.text: Start with bread or baked potato-style recipes before testing pizzas and addon chains. They prove the station structure works without requiring several intermediate ingredients.

docs.title: What Can Go Wrong
docs.text: If a recipe never starts, first confirm the station is the smoker plus stone pressure plate pair. If the station works but a recipe does not match, search the exact output or ingredient with /hl search <query>; many baked foods need an intermediate Heirloom item rather than the raw vanilla ingredient.

docs.title: Espresso Martini
docs.text:
An Espresso Martini uses Coffee Liqueur, and Coffee Liqueur uses espresso you brew yourself. This guide follows the default recipes from coffee cherries to three finished cocktails.

Requires: Heirloom Core, Mixology and Café. Distillery is optional. Server owners can change recipes, so check /hl if your server's ingredients differ.

docs.title: 1. Roast the coffee and pull two Espressos
docs.text:
Use Café's Oven recipes to prepare the beans:

Coffee Cherries → Light Roast Beans → Medium Roast Beans

You can roast medium beans once more for Dark Roast Beans. Either medium or dark beans work for espresso. Put one in the Barista Machine and brew for six seconds. Repeat to make two Espressos: one for the liqueur and one for the final cocktail.

The Oven is a stone pressure plate on a Smoker. The Barista Machine uses an iron trapdoor above quartz stairs. See the Café guide for growing coffee and the other coffee recipes.

docs.title: 2. Make Coffee Liqueur
docs.text:
Add these to the Mixology Table:

Ingredient Amount Espresso 1 Rum 1 Sugar 1

Right-click with an empty hand to start the eight-second shake, then collect one Coffee Liqueur. It is also used in Black Russians, White Russians, Mudslides and B-52s.

docs.title: 3. Shake the Espresso Martini
docs.text:
Add these to the same table:

Ingredient Amount Vodka 1 Coffee Liqueur from step 2 1 The second Espresso 1 Sugar 1 Ice, Packed Ice or Blue Ice 0 or 1 — optional

That is four required ingredients, or five with ice. Use one ice type only. Packed Ice gives a +0.10 quality bonus and Blue Ice +0.20; ordinary Ice has no quality bonus. Ice does not change the alcohol calculation.

Start the shaker, wait eight seconds, then collect three Espresso Martinis. Do not add an extra Glass Bottle. The bottled inputs provide the containers, and other emptied containers are returned by the recipe. Drinking each finished cocktail returns one Glass Bottle.

From the espresso stage onward, the whole chain uses 2 Espressos, 1 Rum, 1 Vodka and 2 Sugar, plus optional ice.

docs.title: Where do the spirits come from?
Without Distillery
docs.text:
Mixology includes these 20-second Boiling Pot recipes:

Output Ingredients Vodka 4 Potatoes + 1 Sugar + 1 Water Bottle Rum 3 Sugar Cane + 1 Sugar + 1 Water Bottle

The Water Bottle supplies the output container; no additional empty bottle is needed. These are the standalone recipes and disappear when compatible Distillery is active.

docs.title: With Distillery
docs.text:
Make a potato-based mash, ferment it and distil it for Vodka. Use a sugar-cane base for Rum. Follow the current Distillery recipe previews in /hl for processing choices and quality guidance. Clicking the spirit ingredient in a Mixology recipe opens its linked production preview.

Your bottles' actual strengths carry through the Coffee Liqueur and the finished Espresso Martini. Mixing shares the batch's alcohol across its three drinks; the recipe does not force every cocktail to a fixed ABV.

Back to Mixology

docs.title: Fruit trees and harvesting
docs.text:
Heirloom Mixology adds fruit trees and palms whose hanging fruit grows visibly as it ripens. Use the addon with its matching Heirloom Core build.

Harvesting ripe coconuts from a palm.

docs.title: Plant and harvest
docs.text:
Plant Lemon, Orange, Mango or Avocado on suitable sapling soil, or a vanilla Apple for an apple tree. Plant Coconut and Bananas on Sand to grow palms. Grove and Tropical starter packets, configurable world drops and chest loot provide survival acquisition routes.

Let hanging fruit ripen, or use bonemeal to advance its growth. Fruit gets visibly bigger as it matures, and harvested nodes begin growing again. Normal protection checks still apply.

A small harvesting trick

You can also knock ripe hanging fruit down with an arrow. Aim at the fruit itself; a successful hit releases one harvest with break particles. The dropped fruit keeps its quality.

Pineapple grows separately as an upright fruit in a short fern. Turn harvested produce into two bottles at the Juicer, then use pure juices at the Mixology Table.

Back to Mixology

docs.title: Juicer
docs.text:
Heirloom Mixology's Juicer blends three fruit or vegetable items into two bottles. Use Heirloom Mixology with a matching Core build that includes the Juicer.

Insert three produce items, blend, then collect both bottles.

docs.title: Build and blend
docs.text:
1. Place a Dropper facing upward, clear Glass above it, and any carpet on top.
  2. Right-click the glass with produce to insert one item at a time. Add exactly three; repeated or mixed ingredients work.
  3. Right-click with an empty hand to start the ten-second blend.
  4. When the liquid settles, right-click with a Glass Bottle to collect one juice. The liquid level falls to half.
  5. Use a second Glass Bottle to collect the remaining juice.

No Water Bottle or bottle insertion is needed before blending. Before the first pour, left-click cancels and refunds the ingredients. After a pour, left-click discards the remaining juice without refunding consumed ingredients.

docs.title: Pure juice and mixed blends
docs.text:
Use three matching produce items for a pure juice used in recipes. Mixed batches blend their colours and list their ingredients. Juice inherits food effects, including harmful ones, and provides half the combined input nutrition. Drinking returns a Glass Bottle.

Choose the three ingredients independently in the in-game recipe browser. Bring your pure juices to the Mixology Table, or grow and harvest fruit.

docs.title: Take it to the bar
docs.text:
Pure juice Example use Tomato Juice Bloody Mary with Vodka, Lemon and Salt Mango or Banana Juice Virgin Daiquiri with Lemon and Sugar Pineapple Juice Shaken Piña Colada with Canned Coconut Milk and Sugar

These recipes need a pure juice made from three matching produce items. A mixed juice containing one tomato is not Tomato Juice. Follow the in-game recipe for optional extras such as ice.

Back to Mixology

docs.title: Mixology Table
docs.text:
Shake cocktails with a moving shaker, particles and synchronized game sounds. Use Heirloom Mixology with a matching Core build that includes the Mixology Table.

Prepare the ingredients, shake, and collect a round of three cocktails.

docs.title: Build and shake
docs.text:
1. Place any wooden pressure plate on an Iron Block.
  2. Find the drink in /hl and right-click the table with its exact ingredients. Extra ingredients do not match.
  3. Right-click with an empty hand to start the eight-second shaker cycle.
  4. Left-click to collect the finished drinks. Left-clicking before completion cancels the batch.

Finished cocktail recipes make three drinks, displayed in a row. Reusable liqueurs and infusions make one bottle. Bottled ingredients supply the recipe containers; follow the in-game recipe rather than adding an extra empty bottle. Other emptied containers return once.

docs.title: A recipe to try
docs.text: With Café installed, try an Espresso Martini. Roast the coffee and pull two Espressos. Use one with Rum and Sugar to make Coffee Liqueur, then shake that liqueur with Vodka, the second Espresso, Sugar and optional ice. The full guide gives the quantities and both spirit-production options.

docs.title: Ingredients and optional addons
docs.text:
Use the Juicer for pure fruit juices. Compatible Distillery supplies genuine brewed spirits, with their actual strength carried into cocktails. Without Distillery, Mixology supplies standalone spirit recipes. Café adds the coffee-based recipes. The recipe browser shows the content available with the addons installed on your server.

Perfect-quality batches have special shaker motions. Recipes that accept ice can use Packed Ice or Blue Ice for a quality bonus; check the ingredient options in /hl.

Back to Mixology

docs.title: Heirloom Mixology
docs.text: Mixology adds fruit trees, fresh juice and cocktails to Heirloom. Grow the ingredients, prepare them at your bar, and use /hl to look up the recipes available on your server.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Fruit trees and harvesting: planting, starter packets and ripening fruit.
  • Juicer: blend three produce items into two bottles, including mixed juices.
  • Mixology Table: build the counter, add ingredients and shake a round of three drinks.
  • Espresso Martini, from the beginning: roast coffee, brew espresso, make Coffee Liqueur and use it in the finished cocktail.

docs.title: Which addons do I need?
docs.text:
Setup What it adds Heirloom Core + Mixology Fruit trees, pineapple, the Juicer, cocktails, mocktails, fruit dishes and standalone spirit recipes Add Café Coffee Liqueur, Espresso Martini, Black Russian, White Russian, Mudslide and B-52 Add compatible Distillery Brewed spirits and wine used by integrated recipes; actual ingredient strength carries through to cocktails, and alcoholic drinks use Distillery's drunkenness system

Café and Distillery are optional. The Espresso Martini example needs Café; it works with or without Distillery. When Distillery is active, its real brewed spirits replace Mixology's standalone spirit recipes. The in-game browser follows the installed addons and server configuration.

Use Mixology with a compatible Core build containing the Mixology Table and Juicer. Install the addon beside Core in plugins/, with the server stopped. No resource pack or client mod is required. See Heirloom installation for the base plugin setup.

docs.title: More from the harvest
docs.text:
Fruit is useful outside the bar. Mixology includes Orange Chicken, Yellow Coconut Curry and Guacamole, and suitable fruit can also be used in Core's jams and ice creams. Guacamole is an optional taco ingredient. Check /hl for the exact ingredients on your server.

Server owners can edit items, recipes and acquisition settings. Mixology's starter packets, world drops and chest loot are configurable rather than compulsory.

docs.title: Interactive station tutorials
docs.text: Use /hl tutorial to choose a cooking lesson. A private scene appears in front of you with full-size blocks at your feet level: blocks assemble, ingredients and tools demonstrate the workflow, and glowing targets wait for your clicks. Only you see and interact with your scene.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install PacketEvents alongside Heirloom to enable tutorials, then restart the server. PacketEvents is optional: without it, Heirloom's cooking, crops, recipes and addons continue to work, and tutorial commands explain the missing dependency. A resource pack is not required.

Tutorials target PacketEvents 2.13.0 on Paper 1.21.11 and 26.2. Server-side verification covers serialized scenes and interactions; final client appearance and interaction feel remain user-run checks.

docs.title: Commands and controls
docs.text:
• /hl tutorial — browse available lessons and completed lessons.
  • /hl tutorial <lesson> — start a lesson; use a short name such as /hl tutorial oven. Tab completion suggests available short names. Qualified IDs remain available when names are ambiguous.
  • /hl tutorial stop — leave the current demonstration.
  • /hld tutorial — browse the Distillery course, when Distillery is installed.

The Heirloom main menu also has a Tutorials card. The heirloom.tutorial permission is granted by default.

The catalogue uses native Minecraft sprite icons beside lesson names. Follow the short action-bar instruction: Left-click (punch) or Right-click, then the action. After eight seconds waiting for a click, a small translated prompt appears above the target. It disappears when you act; timed processing does not show a click prompt. Explanations appear in one caption panel above the scene; longer current-step text pages while the demonstration continues, without delaying the next action. Serving counts update to the latest value. The station-styled progress bar stays visible during work, with the same sweep and shimmer formatting as gameplay. Click guidance remains in the caption while the bar occupies the action row. Chat controls let you go to the previous chapter, replay the current chapter or exit. Left-click or right-click the final emerald to mark a lesson complete; the confirmation is simply “Tutorial complete!”

Start in a clear, loaded area with room for the whole station and space to approach its glowing targets. Every lesson uses the same 1:1 block scale; large stations do not shrink to fit. Pots, stomping tubs and fermenters rest at ground level, with their heat or support shown beneath the floor in a cutaway visible only to you. Use ordinary solid, full-block ground for these lessons. The cutaway preserves floor collision and restores your normal view when the scene closes; it does not remove world blocks. No new configuration is needed.

The scene stays where it began. Move closer when a target is outside normal interaction reach; clicks are checked from your current position. Moving more than 16 blocks from the starting position ends the lesson. Teleporting, changing worlds, dying, logging out, a successful reload or disabling the tutorial dependency also closes the scene. You can start again at any time.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
Core lessons cover the Cutting Board, Mixing Bowl, Oven, Frying Pan and Boiling Pot. Specialized lessons become available with the corresponding active content: Barista Machine, Juicer, Mixology Table and Farmhouse Press. Aging Rack lessons belong to Distillery; Core does not list an aging course.

Distillery lessons cover building and using the Stomping Tub, fermentation cauldron and still, followed by grain preparation, sparkling wine and cellar aging. They also explain station storage, unloaded processing and recovery.

Lessons use the server's current recipes, ingredient amounts and configured times. If an example recipe is unavailable, the base station lesson still teaches construction and controls. Long waits are labelled as accelerated demonstrations and show the real configured duration.

docs.title: Practise aging in the barrel
docs.text:
Use /hl tutorial aging or /hld tutorial aging with Distillery installed. After building the barrel on scaffolding, right-click it to open a practice barrel with the normal 27-slot layout. Move the supplied bottles and planks from the lower inventory into the barrel, then remove the extra wood when prompted. The lesson demonstrates maturation with an accelerated wait and lets you collect the developed bottle.

The lower inventory and cursor in this lesson contain temporary practice items. Your real belongings are preserved, and practice items cannot be kept. Closing the practice window exits the lesson; replay starts with fresh practice items. Read the instruction item in the practice inventory for the current step.

The lesson also explains cellar climate. Ordinary Forest and Taiga biomes provide cool, humid conditions. Nearby water, ice and walls do not change the biome temperature or humidity. You can brew in any biome; ingredients and processing determine the drink family. Wine still ages in other climates; its preferred climate helps craftsmanship. See Cellar Aging for the rack report and maturation routes.

docs.title: Preview behaviour
docs.text:
Station previews reuse production placement, animation, particle and progress helpers. The Oven course shows the required smoker and stone pressure plate, followed by an optional brick shell built one block at a time and the rear fire used during baking. Each required part is placed by a click, ingredients travel into the station, and collected items jump upward and toward you. The chopping sword and mixing shovel stay close above the actual work surface: the sword moves down toward the board, and the shovel follows a tight stirring motion over the bowl. Forward steps retain the existing station displays; Replay and Previous reconstruct their checkpoint. Items keep their station orientation when you look around.

Tutorial blocks, items, click targets and practice inventories are private displays. They do not build real stations, spend ingredients, grant food, change brewing history or start real timers. Tutorial completion IDs are the only saved gameplay change.

A failed configuration reload retains the prior lesson registrations. A successful reload closes active scenes so the next lesson uses current definitions. Scenes belonging to removed addons close safely.

Tutorial narration has priority over Heirloom's background drunkenness reminders until the lesson ends. Other plugins may still show their own action-bar messages; simultaneous tutorials from different plugins are not coordinated.

Tutorial copy is bundled for all 26 supported server locales. Choose the usual server locale; administrator keys in Core or addon lang/<locale>.yml override the bundled text. Most existing instructions, controls and progress labels have machine-authored translations, which have not had a full native-speaker review. The new barrel-practice instructions and rack-report text currently use English fallbacks in non-English locales. Custom item names retain their configured names, and dynamic vanilla item names passed into a sentence may also appear in English.

Native sprite components use the Minecraft text API introduced in 1.21.9; no icon resource pack is needed. The supported server baseline remains Paper 1.21.11. See Adventure's sprite component API.
